Three freehold retail units on Greenwood Avenue in Bukit Timah for sale at $18.5 mil
article:
Three freehold ground-floor retail units at 20, 26 and 28 Greenwood Avenue in Bukit Timah are on the market with a combined guide price of $18.5 million.

CBRE, the exclusive marketing agent for the asset, said buyers have the option to purchase them individually or as a portfolio.

The property at 20 Greenwood Avenue has a guide price of $6.5 million, or $4,224 psf on its strata area of 1,539 sq ft.

The properties at 26 and 28 Greenwood Avenue are neighbouring units. Spanning 1,442 and 1,475 sq ft, they are priced at $6 million apiece, which works out to $4,161 psf and $4,068 psf, respectively.

All three units are currently fully tenanted.

The properties are situated within the Hillcrest Park landed enclave, where ownership of commercial units “remains highly exclusive”, with just 27 units across the entire estate, said CBRE.

Despite this tightly held supply, it has drawn a strong mix of established operators — from F&B names such as Baker & Cook, Peperoni Pizzeria, Greenwood Fish Market and Bacaro, to supermarket chains like Cold Storage and FairPrice Xpress.

Based on caveats lodged, the most recent commercial property transaction at Greenwood Avenue was for a 1,539 sq ft unit that changed hands for $7.1 million ($4,613 psf) in July this year.

Following that transaction, the guide price of $6 million to $6.5 million per unit for the properties up for sale presents a discount of approximately 10% to 18% to the latest market benchmark, said Clemence Lee, executive director for capital markets at CBRE Singapore.

He added: “Given this value, we anticipate strong interest from high-net-worth investors and family offices, as well as owner-occupiers such as boutique retailers and bespoke food and beverage operators who are looking to secure a foothold in this highly sought-after freehold enclave”.

With Turf City set to add up to 20,000 new homes, demand for F&B and lifestyle offerings in enclaves like Hillcrest Park is set to grow — while freehold commercial space in Bukit Timah remains scarce, with no known new supply planned.

This mix of rising demand and fixed supply makes it a compelling bet for investors seeking rental resilience and long-term capital appreciation, said Lee.

The units are up for sale through an expression of interest exercise that will close at 3pm on Sept 23.

title: Fairmont brand debuts in Thailand with Fairmont Bangkok Sukhumvit
article:
Fairmont Hotels & Resorts, part of hospitality firm Accor, has announced the opening of Fairmont Bangkok Sukhumvit — the brand’s first hotel in Thailand. The hotel was opened on Aug 18 in partnership with Thai integrated lifestyle real estate group Asset World Corp.

Situated in Bangkok's Sukhumvit neighbourhood, the hotel offers 416 guestrooms and 58 suites. Interiors were helmed by Thailand-based architectural and design firm PIA, delivering a modern take on the country's botanical heritage.

The lobby's centrepiece is a chandelier inspired by Thailand's national flower, crafted from 4,166 glass pieces and over 35,000 crystal balls. Bespoke artworks, sculptural forms and subtle botanical motifs are woven into the design of guestrooms and public spaces.

Pet-friendly amenities and a Kids Club programme are available.

Dining venues at the hotel include North American-French brasserie Harper's, Aela Social Bar and Caya Pool Club. Additionally, entertainment destination Wiggle Room is set to open later this year.

Guests can enjoy treatments at the Fairmont Spa or work out at Fairmont Studio, which offers dedicated spaces for yoga, cardio and strength training. Rounding out the offering is Fairmont Fit, which extends wellness beyond the gym and spa through programming and other touchpoints.

Fairmont Bangkok Sukhumvit also offers over 21,500 sq ft of flexible event space across three floors.

title: 3 SGX Dividend Stocks Rewarding Shareholders This Week
article:
Three dividend payments will reach Singapore investors’ accounts inside 72 hours this week.
Singapore Telecommunications
(SGX: Z74) pays on 19 August 2026;
iFAST Corporation
(SGX: AIY) follows a day later; and
Keppel Ltd
(SGX: BN4) pays last on 21 August 2026.
The calendar makes the three look alike, but the cash behind them differs sharply.
Every
dividend
draws on money the business generated or raised.
Some of that money arrives again next year.
Some of it comes from selling an asset the company will never own twice.
Free cash flow keeps the dividend tap running.
The type of cash doing the work decides whether the payout holds.
The three payers sit at different points on that spectrum.
iFAST
raised its payout
, and rising profit covered the increase.
Singtel splits its dividend into two components drawn from separate sources, while Keppel held its payout unchanged as operating cash flow more than halved.
Is iFAST’s dividend increase backed by profit?
iFAST declared a second interim dividend of S$0.03, 50% higher than the S$0.02 paid a year ago.
Profit growth paid for that increase.
Revenue rose 34.8% year on year (YoY) to S$162.0 million in the second quarter of 2026 (2Q2026).
First-half revenue grew 39.3% to S$316.5 million.
Net profit attributable to owners climbed 40.7% YoY to S$57.9 million for the half.
Assets under administration reached a record S$36.13 billion as at 30 June 2026, up 32.8% YoY.
Net inflows contributed S$2.56 billion during the half.
Recurring net revenue accounted for 90.2% of non-banking net revenue.
Free cash flow fell to S$140.9 million in 1H2026 from S$435.8 million.
The two figures do not compare like-for-like.
Customer deposit movements at iFAST Global Bank run through operating cash flow, and the prior-year base carried a larger deposit increase.
Net cash stood at S$384.7 million at the end of June.
Management raised full-year dividend guidance to S$0.12 or higher.
What is actually funding Singtel’s dividend?
Singtel’s 19 August payment is the final instalment of its FY2026 dividend.
That fiscal year ended 31 March 2026 (FY2026).
The results behind this payment cover a different period from the June-end figures at iFAST and Keppel.
Management declared a total ordinary dividend of S$0.185 per share for FY2026, up 9% compared with a year ago.
A core dividend of S$0.134 tracks underlying earnings, while a value realisation dividend of S$0.051 draws on capital recycling – Singtel sold a 0.8% stake in Airtel for S$1.5 billion during the year.
Underlying net profit rose 12% YoY to S$2.8 billion.
That figure anchors the core component.
Group revenue held stable at S$14.3 billion as a 2% depreciation in the Australian dollar masked underlying growth.
NCS lifted operating profit 34% to S$340 million and secured a record S$3.8 billion in bookings.
Optus added 23% to reach A$550 million.
Singtel Singapore moved the other way.
Operating profit there fell 4.6% to S$795 million amid mobile competition and eSIM pressure on roaming revenue.
Net debt gearing stood at 23.3%.
Can Keppel’s cash flow carry an unchanged dividend?
Keppel
declared an interim dividend of S$0.150 per share, unchanged from a year ago.
Revenue for 1H2026 rose 24.6% YoY to S$3.8 billion.
Infrastructure drove the gain with a 27% rise to S$2.5 billion after the Keppel Sakra Cogen Plant began commercial operations.
Net profit attributable to shareholders fell 59.0% to S$154.7 million after a S$375 million loss in the non-core portfolio.
Net profit excluding that portfolio rose 25% to S$530 million.
Recurring income grew 13% to S$467 million.
The dividend question sits in the cash flow statement.
Operating cash flow fell to S$96.8 million from S$219.4 million a year ago on higher working capital needs.
The company reported a free cash inflow of S$570 million, which included investing activities and came largely from S$1.1 billion of divestment proceeds and dividends received.
Keppel has announced about S$1.7 billion of asset monetisation year to date against a full-year target of S$2 billion to S$3 billion.
Cash stood at S$2.2 billion as at 30 June 2026, against borrowings of S$11.3 billion excluding lease liabilities.
Get Smart: Trace the cash before you count the income
Three payment dates in three days tell you nothing about durability; the
cash flow statement
does.
When a dividend arrives, work backwards to the line that funded it.
Recurring revenue that grew this year tends to show up again next year.
Proceeds from selling a stake or a rig will not repeat once the asset is gone.
Singtel makes the distinction easy by naming its two components separately.
Most companies leave that work to you.
None of this makes capital recycling wrong.
Keppel runs its monetisation programme deliberately, and the proceeds fund a shift towards asset management.
A payout leaning on divestments depends on how many assets remain to sell.
A payout leaning on recurring revenue depends on customers staying put.
Work out which of the two your dividend rests on.
Then decide how much weight you are willing to place on it.
Many Singapore stocks fall behind inflation, which means your money quietly loses strength over time. Dividend stocks have a very different track record. Some continued delivering 6% to 13% every year across the toughest market conditions.

title: Alphabet’s 7% Aussie bond debut underscores the sky-high cost of AI debt
article:
(Aug19): Alphabet Inc paid just under 7% to borrow longer-dated funds in its debut Australian dollar bond offering, its highest-ever for a note, underscoring how broader demands for cash among hyperscalers around the world are feeding into more costly funding almost everywhere.

The US tech giant sold A$5.5 billion of debt Wednesday in a multi-part deal, with the yield on the 20-year tranche, the longest part, set at 6.98%, according to an email from Australia & New Zealand Banking Group, one of the banks leading the sale. The deal attracted demand in excess of A$18 billion, the bank said.

The elevated borrowing costs for even Alphabet are more a reflection of the multi-decade high yields seen around the world this week than of the creditworthiness of Google’s parent company, which has S&P Global Ratings’ second-highest credit score. Rekindled inflation and a glut of fundraising by both governments and large tech firms, in general, are stoking concern about the capacity of investors to absorb the debt and pushing up the cost of doing so.

Still, the hundreds of billions of dollars being raised by Big Tech this year to finance their AI ambitions is fanning concerns that such fundraising, possibly in its early innings, will syphon away demand from government debt, exacerbating fiscal concerns. Alphabet trails only Amazon.com Inc so far in 2026 among large US corporates in tapping global debt markets across currencies.

“Investors recognised they were being offered an attractive entry point into one of the world’s strongest corporate balance sheets,” said Chamath De Silva, head of fixed income at Betashares. He expects Amazon to be the next hyperscaler to tap the Australian market.

See also: AI’s lucrative jobs boom is leaving women behind globally

Corporate debt typically is priced over government debt or benchmarks heavily influenced by movements in rates, which means that companies generally end up paying more to borrow too when sovereigns do. Yields on 30-year US Treasuries rose to the highest since 2007 this week while French and German borrowing costs also hit multi-year highs.

Alphabet paid a spread of 180 basis points over the local benchmark to borrow A$1 billion for 20 years in the deal, according to ANZ. The single largest tranche was a A$1.5 billion floating-rate note that also attracted the most orders, the bank said.

title: AI boom, energy shocks see Southeast Asia's growth bifurcate
article:
(Aug 19): Vietnam retained its crown as Southeast Asia’s fastest-growing major economy in the second quarter, with Thailand the laggard, as tech and energy dictated varied fortunes across the region.

Malaysia and Singapore were the second- and third-quickest expanding, helped by robust demand for semiconductors and other components used in global technology supply chains.

Along with Thailand, the Philippines was also more exposed to surging energy costs stemming from conflict in the Middle East. A sharp pullback in infrastructure spending additionally weighed on growth in the Philippines.

The divergence underscores Southeast Asia’s reputation as an increasingly important alternative to China for manufactured exports. However it also highlights the uneven benefits of that shift, as economies with companies crucial to the AI-related technology supply chain prove more resilient, while those more vulnerable to expensive imported energy lose momentum.

Policymakers across the region are now grappling with how to cushion businesses and consumers from volatile oil prices without undermining economic growth.

See also: Southeast Asia to see hot, dry weather and increased fire risk

“Growth diverged across countries, dictated by the degree of domestic resilience in the face of the Middle East crisis and the share of exposure to technology exports” within the trade mix, DBS Group Holdings Ltd economists Chua Han Teng and Radhika Rao said.

Expansion will probably only continue to bifurcate given the unresolved conflict in the Middle East and sustained global demand for technology exports spurred by artificial intelligence (AI)-related hardware.

Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp (OCBC) on Wednesday upgraded its full-year forecasts for Vietnam and Indonesia to 8.2% and 5.2% respectively. The Philippines’ outlook was downgraded to 3.2% from 3.8% while Thailand was nudged slightly higher to 2.4%, thanks to a stronger private sector buoyed by increased data centre investments.

See also: Thailand plans to scrap US$29.7 bil land-bridge project bypassing Malacca Strait after study

“Despite differing fiscal policy responses to higher global oil prices, the balance of revisions remains skewed towards growth upgrades rather than downgrades,” economists led by Lavanya Venkateswaran wrote. “This supports our view that monetary policy across the region is likely to remain on a tightening path.”

Singapore, meanwhile, upgraded its 2026 economic growth forecast earlier this month as the AI boom lifted trade and manufacturing, offsetting the drag from the war in Iran.

“The global AI investment boom has been stronger than expected,” the Ministry of Trade and Industry said in a statement. “For the rest of the year, a further acceleration in AI-related capital expenditure is expected to lift the growth prospects of economies plugged into the global technology value chain.”

title: Virgin Atlantic and Trainline face UK probe over misleading retail pricing
article:
(Aug19): Virgin Atlantic Airways Ltd and Trainline plc face an investigation from the UK watchdog over misleading retail pricing, in the first move since the country’s new prime minister promised to ease the cost of living for consumers.

The Competition and Markets Authority started three consumer-protection investigations on Wednesday, including against Red Driving School, over concerns that customers were not shown the total price upfront — a practice known as drip pricing. The watchdog suspects the firms did not include mandatory fees for services in the upfront cost shown to customers.

“Investigations into online pricing practices are part of CMA’s work to help ease cost-of-living pressures,” the regulator said in a statement.

The announcement comes just a week after UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham embarked on a nationwide tour to promote new policies aimed at reducing the cost of living. He pledged “everyday fixes” for issues that contribute to higher prices for consumers.

“Mandatory fees are indicated at multiple stages throughout the booking journey. We are reviewing the points raised by the CMA carefully,” Virgin Atlantic Holidays said in a statement.

Trainline has engaged with the CMA and is “taking steps to enhance the presentation of certain fees", the company said.

See also: The post-pandemic travel boom is finally losing steam

The opening of the investigation does not mean the firms have broken the law. If the probe eventually finds breaches, the CMA can seek compensation for consumers and impose fines worth as much as 10% of a firm’s global revenue.

title: Hong Kong bourse posts record earnings on IPO, trading boom
article:
(Aug 19): Hong Kong’s stock exchange beat market estimates with a 21% rise in second-quarter net income, fuelled by robust trading volumes and a jump in initial public offerings (IPOs).

Hong Kong Exchanges & Clearing Ltd (HKEX) reported record net income of HK$5.38 billion (US$686 million or $876 million) in the three months ended June, according to a statement on Wednesday. That compared with a consensus estimate of HK$4.91 billion, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Core business revenue rose 17% in the quarter as trading and IPOs extended a winning streak, the exchange said.

“Looking ahead, despite persistent macro and geopolitical uncertainties, the long-term opportunity for HKEX and for Hong Kong remains compelling as global capital increasingly seeks access to China’s innovation economy and Asia’s growth prospects,” said chief executive officer Bonnie Chan, whose contract was renewed this week for a three-year term from March 2027.

HKEX shares rose as much as 1.6% in the early afternoon session in Hong Kong.

The exchange has been delivering record earnings as the city has benefitted from Chinese companies linked to the artificial intelligence build-out moving Hong Kong deals to a higher gear. However, analysts are increasingly focusing on the company’s expansion of its non-equity business.

Hong Kong’s market regulator has also stepped up warnings to investment banks over filing sloppy applications for share sales. HKEX’s shares are little changed so far this year in a weak broader market.

See also: Hong Kong Exchanges non-equity push seen key for stock boost

IPO volumes rose 94% in the first half of the year, with 87 companies raising HK$212.4 billion. The bourse ranks second globally after Nasdaq.

Meanwhile, trading via the Stock Connect links with mainland China hit records. The exchange added eight more exchange-traded funds to the southbound link, bringing the total to 31 as of the end of June.

China announced on Tuesday it will support mainland insurance firms to invest in exchange-traded funds via the southbound Stock Connect.

title: CXMT rival YMTC moves closer to China’s next big chip IPO
article:
(Aug19): Yangtze Memory Technologies Co moved closer to an initial public offering in China, following in the footsteps of rival CXMT Corp’s near-record share sale.

The company known as YMTC completed its pre-listing tutoring work and was found to have the corporate governance structure, accounting foundation and internal control systems expected of a listed company, according to a report published on the China Securities Regulatory Commission’s website.

YMTC is now on track to follow CXMT’s fundraising example as China’s homegrown chip giants look to tap capital markets to expand capacity and bolster Beijing’s drive for tech self-sufficiency. CXMT last month raised 66.6 billion yuan, the second-biggest mainland debut ever, and became the country’s largest listed company as its shares surged out of the gate.

The news was partly blamed for a selloff in Chinese technology stocks, as large IPOs are typically seen as draining market liquidity and weighing on investor sentiment. The STAR 50 Index plunged 6.9% on Wednesday, its biggest drop in a month.

“The global weakness in tech stocks and the pace of IPOs — with news of YMTC coming on the heels of Unitree — also have something to do with it, though they are not the core factors,” said Niu Chunbao, fund manager at Shanghai Wanji Asset Management Co.

YMTC and CXMT are central to Beijing’s strategic priorities as artificial intelligence demand drives a global memory shortage and soaring profits across the industry. Their importance has increased under US export curbs, fuelling investor bets on China’s domestic chip supply chain and sending related stocks sharply higher.

See also: Ant Group said to sell 3% Paytm stake in US$309 mil deal

YMTC has edged out Japan’s Kioxia Holdings Corp to become the world’s third-biggest provider of flash memory shipments during the June quarter, a sign that Chinese chipmakers are benefiting from AI-driven shortages. It also narrowed its gap with Samsung Electronics Co and SK Hynix Inc in terms of global NAND bit shipment volume.

title: South Korea exploring new financial hub beyond overcrowded Seoul
article:
(Aug 19): South Korea is looking to create a new financial centre outside the capital Seoul, as the government moves to ease over-concentration in the greater metropolitan area, which is home to more than half the country’s population.

One candidate being considered is Jeonbuk, a province about 200 kilometres south of Seoul, which is already home to the National Pension Service, which manages more than US$1 trillion ($1.28 trillion). The NPS relocated its headquarters to Jeonbuk in 2015.

At a committee meeting, government officials and financial industry leaders discussed a plan to develop a new financial hub, including how to evaluate whether Jeonbuk was a suitable candidate, the Financial Services Commission said in a statement on Wednesday.

The drive by the administration of President Lee Jae Myung to balance overall national development and ease the concentration of business, people, and jobs in Seoul mirrors steps elsewhere to establish additional financial and administrative hubs.

Japanese lawmakers approved a bill in July to designate one or more regions as a backup if Tokyo is incapacitated by a disaster. China called earlier this year for greater efforts to develop the metropolis of Xiongan near Beijing to serve as a release valve for the crowded capital. In India, authorities are pushing for further development of GIFT City, a financial hub that’s several hours away by air from the traffic-choked streets of Mumbai.

The government will “encourage financial market innovation, establish infrastructure that complies with global standards, and vitalise the capital market to be more foreign investor friendly”, to foster a solid financial hub, the statement said.

See also: Frasers lifts stake in German fashion house Hugo Boss to 48%

The committee will also “actively support” the overseas expansion of local financial institutions and boost communication with global financial firms operating in South Korea.

A panel made up of officials, academics and industry experts will evaluate Jeonbuk’s potential to grow into a global financial hub and its ability to attract domestic and international financial institutions. The government has also announced plans to build a massive new chip hub in the far south of the country.

In 2009, South Korea designated Seoul and Busan as financial hubs. Seoul ranked eighth and Busan the 23rd financial hub globally in March this year, according to the Global Financial Centres Index 39.

title: HSBC rides wave of China’s surging trade links with Brazil
article:
(Aug 19): Brazil’s record trading volume with China is proving to be a boon to HSBC Holdings plc, a decade after the bank sold its sprawling Brazilian operation and then returned to focus on the cross-border business that has become a sweet spot.

Trade-finance booked in Hong Kong for Brazilian companies was almost immaterial for HSBC from a revenue standpoint just three years ago. Last year, it ranked 10th among firms from the 50 nations that book trade-finance deals in Hong Kong using HSBC. Now it’s the fourth-biggest, according to Alexandre Guião, the bank’s chief executive officer for Brazil.

“Brazil’s exports of hard and soft commodities, as well as imports from Asia, mainly China, have been growing a lot,” Guião said in an interview at the UK bank’s Sao Paulo offices. “We want to make sure that we facilitate those connections” between companies from those regions, he said.

Revenue from Brazilian customers surged 20% last year, including deals booked offshore, Guião said, adding that the figure soared an additional 37% in the first half of this year.

The reason is clear: Brazil’s exports to China jumped 20% this year through July, to a record US$69 billion ($88 billion), according to the Brazilian government. Meanwhile, imports increased by 8%, to an all-time high of US$45 billion, fuelled by a wave of electrified vehicles. Brazil received more investments from China than any other country last year, according to the Brazil-China Business Council.

As the biggest foreign bank in China, HSBC is especially well positioned to gain from those closer relations.

See also: DBS planning successor for long-term chairman Seah — Bloomberg

The situation was different 10 years ago. HSBC sold its local subsidiary to Banco Bradesco SA in 2016, and then returned two and a half years later, after a non-compete period, with an operation that’s now a complete corporate and investment bank. It serves about 720 global multinationals in the nation and about 80 Brazilian multinationals.

Globally, HSBC is selling businesses and shrinking and revamping its operations, part of a major restructuring that includes cutting billions in expenses. The idea is to simplify the company, concentrate capital where HSBC has structural advantages, push harder into wealth and Asia-linked flows, and use artificial intelligence to cut costs and improve customer service.

In Latin America, that meant selling its Uruguay unit in 2025 to Banco BTG Pactual SA for US$175 million and divesting the Argentina subsidiary in 2024 to Grupo Financiero Galicia for US$550 million.

See also: Standard Chartered revamps leveraged finance team to focus on sponsors

In Mexico, where HSBC kept a full bank including a retail business, the lender decided to focus on wealthier clients and closed about 200 branches in 18 months, according to Jorge Arce, the bank’s CEO and president for Mexico and head of Latin American operations.

HSBC also has a bank in Chile, “a very important nation for the Asia corridor with Latin America”, Arce said, while in Colombia it has an office that also covers Peru.

Among HSBC’s recent deals was a US$1.5 billion financing package, which it lead along with International Finance Corp, for Mubadala Capital’s renewable energy arm, Acelen Renewables, to build a greenfield biorefinery in Bahia, Brazil.

But there have been hiccups. Big debt restructurings in Brazil from companies such as sugar and ethanol producer Raizen and supermarket chain GPA, known as Cia. Brasileira de Distribuicao, weighed on HSBC’s profit. But Guião said that was more than outweighed by the revenue growth.

After those debt restructurings, HSBC paused to review its portfolio and decided to become more conservative in offering credit, he said.

Arce called those issues “part of the business”, adding that “at the end of the day, I think the debt workouts from those companies are going to be positive for lenders”.

Brazil’s stubbornly high interest rates “make you feel cautious,” Arce said, but he added that Brazilian companies “are very resilient”. Brazil’s benchmark interest rate has been at or above 14% for more than a year.

The high cost of funding and “a credit crunch” for some companies in Brazil’s local market also created opportunities for HSBC, which increased the volume of bilateral loans booked outside Brazil, Guião said. Cash management, payments and foreign-exchange businesses for Brazilian clients are also expanding, he said.

The plan is to keep investing in Brazil, despite the uncertainties raised by October’s presidential elections, both executives said.

“No matter who wins, Brazil will continue to be a very attractive market for our clients, and we are going to be here serving them,” Arce said.

title: MAS introduces measures to incentivise key asset managers to establish or deepen presence in Singapore
article:
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has announced a set of three measures in a bid to incentivise key asset managers to anchor their business activities, capital allocation and talent deployment in Singapore.

These include a proposed tax exemption introduced by the central bank and the Ministry of Finance for profit-related returns from qualifying funds, a new hedge fund investment programme, and a new investment management track under the Overseas Networks & Expertise (ONE) Pass framework.

The announcement comes a day after the Hong Kong government issued a new bill to cut taxes for hedge funds, although Singapore does not see the competition with the special administrative region (SAR) as a “zero sum” game, says National Development Minister Chee Hong Tat, who is also deputy chairman of the MAS.

“We believe that the region is big enough. There’s enough scope for both cities to grow as financial sectors,” he adds at a doorstop on Aug 19.

On the first measure, the proposed tax exemption will apply to a share of investment profits earned by fund managers and investment professionals when they deliver “strong returns” for investors in qualifying funds.

These funds refer to those which qualify for tax exemptions under Sections 13D, 13O, 13OA, 13U, and 13V of the Income Tax Act 1947 and are managed by Singapore-based fund managers. Such fund managers are already required to meet requirements such as a minimum headcount.

See also: Singapore's AUM grew 10% in 2025 to $6.7 trillion

This measure is expected to take effect from the Year of Assessment in 2027, covering income earned in 2026. More details will be announced at Budget 2027, which has consistently been the practice when it comes to changes to Singapore’s tax rules and policies, says Chee.

The new hedge fund investment programme, says MAS, will invest with hedge fund managers “committed to establishing or deepening their presence in Singapore”.

The programme will also support the growth of Singapore’s hedge fund investment ecosystem including ancillary service providers and prime brokerages. More details will be shared when ready, the central bank adds.

See also: Ascend Asia Asset Management launches new credit investment strategy

Finally, the new investment management track will be targeted towards global leaders and senior investment professionals who “have the potential to contribute or are already contributing significantly to Singapore’s asset management industry”.

The track may include refining the assessment of salaries to “better reflect established compensation structures” in the industry such as recognising returns linked to investment performance and fund outcomes.

The ONE pass was announced in August 2022 and launched in January 2023 in a bid to attract talent across sectors including business, arts and culture, sports, academia and research.

Under the existing framework, applicants will need to have a fixed monthly salary of $30,000 under an employer for 12 straight months leading to the date of application. These applicants will also have to earn the same sum under a Singapore-based company, which has to have a market capitalisation of at least US$500 million or annual revenue of at least US$200 million.

Singapore’s asset management industry is a key growth engine for the city-state's financial sector, accounting for around 15% of the sector’s output and 13% of its employment.

Over the past five years, the industry grew positively by 7.5% per year on average to almost $7 trillion. The sector also provides close to 25,000 jobs, of which 80% are filled by locals.

title: DBS planning successor for long-term chairman Seah — Bloomberg
article:
(Aug 19): DBS Group Holdings Ltd is working on a succession plan for Peter Seah, who has been the Singapore bank’s chairman for more than 16 years, according to people with knowledge of the matter.

Seah, 79, has fulfilled his responsibilities in guiding the country’s largest bank since he joined the DBS board in 2009 and became chairman a year later, said the people, who asked not to be identified discussing private matters.

Seah, a non-executive chairman, is also chairman of the board executive committee and DBS’ Hong Kong unit. In addition, he is a member of the audit, board risk management, technology, compensation, management development and nominating committees, according to DBS’ website. Seah was re-elected as chairman at the most recent annual shareholders’ meeting in March.

“Mr Peter Seah remains non-executive chairman of DBS Group Holdings,” the bank said in response to queries from Bloomberg.

A veteran banker with many senior roles, Seah is credited for being instrumental in driving the growth of DBS, thanks to his good working relationship with former bank chief executive officer Piyush Gupta and his successor Tan Su Shan. Over recent months, DBS’ stock price has soared, backed by strong earnings and a thriving wealth management business, catapulting the lender to become one of the world’s largest banks by market value.

The Ministry of Manpower said on Wednesday that Seah is resigning from his chairman post at the National Wages Council for personal reasons.

See also: Standard Chartered revamps leveraged finance team to focus on sponsors

Seah has also been the chairman of Singapore Airlines Ltd since 2017. The city-state’s flagship carrier said in July 2025 when Seah was re-elected that it was “critical” he remains on its board as non-independent and non-executive chairman to provide leadership and continuity as the company navigates global uncertainties and challenges ahead.

Elsewhere, he sits on the board of GIC Pte Ltd, Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund. He is also a member of the country’s Council of Presidential Advisers. A banker for more than three decades, Seah was CEO of the former Overseas Union Bank until 2001.

title: LG Energy mulls supplying batteries for US drones in pivot
article:
(Aug 19): LG Energy Solution Ltd is considering supplying the US government and major defence contractors with batteries for drones and other unmanned weapons systems to capture growing demand for military hardware as demand from electric vehicles (EVs) sputters.

The South Korean battery maker has received inquiries from multiple potential American partners about defence opportunities, Bob Lee, the company’s president for North America, said in an interview.

Although discussions are in their early stages, expanding into defence would mark a significant strategic shift for the LG group, which has historically avoided the sector. It also highlights a broader move into defence by commercial companies as the Trump administration pushes to replenish munitions used in the Iran and Ukraine wars, and strengthen domestic supply chains for drones and other strategic technologies.

“Defence is a very big source of funding and business opportunities right now, so we are getting some inquiries,” Lee said. “We are being very careful in terms of how we manage that.”

Lee likened LG’s past stance on defence to consumer companies deciding not to get into alcohol or tobacco. But now, “we definitely see growth and opportunities”, he said.

LG shares rose as much as 2.6% in Seoul on Wednesday, while the nation’s benchmark Kospi index fell.

See also: Korea denies report on discussing chips as first US investment

The pivot comes as LG reorients its business in North America after an expected jump in EV adoption failed to materialise. Energy storage is now the majority of its US business, while EV batteries dominate outside the US, Lee said.

The company is quickly expanding in the energy storage market where demand for infrastructure upgrades and from AI data centres is surging. It has repurposed five of its eight plants in the region initially built to support EVs for the energy storage market. Lee said the company expects that business to be profitable by the end of the year.

LG on Tuesday hosted a ceremony to mark the opening of a Lansing, Michigan, battery plant built through a partnership with General Motors Co. The site will now supply about US$4.3 billion ($5.5 billion) worth of lithium-iron-phosphate cells for Tesla Inc’s Megapack energy storage systems starting in 2027.

See also: Alibaba to sell gaming arm for US$1.5 bil in boost to AI pivot

LG’s Lansing plant will also produce nickel-based battery cells for Toyota Motor Corp vehicles, after transferring a US$1.5 billion order from another LG plant in Holland, Michigan. That site in turn will manufacture energy storage cells for Michigan utility DTE Energy.

The Lansing plant’s annual capacity is expected to reach 35 gigawatt-hours by the end of next year.

LG’s expansion of its US manufacturing footprint comes amid new tensions between the US and South Korean governments over trade and security. US President Donald Trump has scaled back military exercises planned with South Korea while praising North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Trump administration officials have also complained that Seoul is slow-walking a pledge to invest US$350 billion into the US.

Still, South Korean companies continue to win orders from America, with the US Army selecting a unit of Hanwha Aerospace Co to provide the new Mobile Tactical Cannon, in a deal worth up to US$262 million that could eventually turn into a larger contract to replace the Army’s ageing M777 towed howitzers.

The Trump administration last week announced tariffs of as much as 100% on imported drones and their components, a move that could speed a US decoupling of drone supply chains from China.

China is also a major competitor in energy-storage batteries. LG’s Lee said he urged US Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who attended Tuesday’s event in Lansing, to consider measures that would restrict Chinese access to the energy storage market.

“It’s very important for us to become more independent and be self-reliant,” Lee said. “He was very much on board.”

South Korea’s battery makers have been repurposing factory capacity for grid storage after North American carmakers dialled back EV plans and unwound joint ventures.

Samsung SDI Co is acquiring General Motors' stake in an Indiana venture and converting the facility for energy storage production. SK On, the battery unit of SK Innovation Co, will operate a Tennessee plant for stationary battery output that it had developed through a now-defunct partnership with Ford Motor Co.

Michael Sanders, a senior adviser at research firm Avicenne Energy, said there is “very limited chance” of excess capacity in the US battery market through 2035 or 2040.

“The big question is how long the data centre hype will live on,” Sanders said in an email. “But between energy storage systems and EV demand, even if it loses a little lustre we don’t need to worry about oversupply.”

title: Gold edges higher as US bond yields stabilise after surge
article:
(Aug 19): Gold rose as a selloff in US bonds eased, relieving pressure on the precious metal after it fell the most in almost a month on Tuesday.

Bullion climbed as much as 0.6% to trade above US$4,360 an ounce, after shedding almost 2% in the previous session. Treasuries steadied following a plunge that sent yields on 30-year notes to the highest in almost two decades on Tuesday. Higher borrowing costs are typically negative for gold, which doesn’t pay interest.

Gold has recovered in recent weeks to trade around US$4,400 an ounce, supported by renewed investor demand and central-bank buying, notably from China. A fund manager survey by Bank of America Corp on Tuesday showed gold hit the highest level since March 2023.

The dimming prospects for a peace deal between the US and Iran may keep a lid on further gains, however. US President Donald Trump insisted on Tuesday that there were no talks ongoing with Tehran, leaving control of the Strait of Hormuz in limbo. The memorandum of understanding the two countries signed in June has expired with no plan to extend it, buoying oil prices. Energy-led inflation puts pressure on the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates, a headwind for bullion.

While there may not be “renewed selling pressure, the recent surge in flows into precious metals appears to be easing,” Ryan McKay, an analyst from TD Securities, wrote in a note.

See also: Bank of Korea makes first gold-linked investment in 13 years

The next clues on the Fed’s rate path will come later Wednesday with the release of the minutes from its July policy meeting, followed by chairman Kevin Warsh’s speech to the Fed’s annual Jackson Hole symposium next week.

Spot gold was 0.5% higher at US$4,357.07 an ounce at 11.34 am in Singapore. Silver fell 0.6% to US$62.99 an ounce. Platinum and palladium edged higher. The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index, a gauge of the US currency, declined 0.1%.

title: Standard Chartered revamps leveraged finance team to focus on sponsors
article:
(Aug 19): Standard Chartered plc has reorganised its leveraged acquisition finance team as part of a push to sharpen focus on funding sponsor-led deals.

The bank’s leveraged acquisition finance group is now headed by David Law, who has been appointed as the global head of sponsor financing and private credit, a spokesperson for the firm said in response to a query from Bloomberg News.

London-based Law was previously the head of leveraged and acquisition finance and private credit for Europe and Americas, according to the spokesperson. Jujhar Singh, who was in charge of the leveraged and acquisition finance team, is still with the bank, the spokesperson said.

Financing responsibility for corporate clients under the leveraged acquisition finance business is now under Surya Bagchi, the global head of financing solutions, according to the spokesperson. “The changes are intended to strengthen our financing platform, enhance connectivity across teams and better support clients’ evolving financing needs.”

Standard Chartered’s move is taking place at a time when deal-making is increasing and firms are looking to deploy more capital. Investors have been particularly drawn to sectors like digital infrastructure and healthcare, while private equity firms are also in hot pursuit of acquisitions.

title: Ant Group said to sell 3% Paytm stake in US$309 mil deal
article:
(Aug 19): Resilient Asset Management BV, controlled by Paytm founder Vijay Shekhar Sharma, on Tuesday sold a 3% stake in the Indian fintech for US$309 million ($395 million), according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified.

The proceeds from the transaction will flow to Ant Group Co under an agreement reached three years ago, according to an exchange filing Paytm made late on Monday.

The stake is part of the 10.3% interest the Netherlands-based Resilient acquired from Jack Ma-backed Ant Group in August 2023 in exchange for convertible securities rather than cash. The arrangement allows the Chinese fintech to retain the economic benefit from the shares.

On Tuesday, about 19.2 million shares, or 2.99% of the company’s equity changed hands in three pre-market block trades, exchange data showed. The deal took place at 1,535.10 rupees per share, generating proceeds of 29.5 billion rupees (US$309 million or $395 million), according to Bloomberg calculations. The stock fell 2.2% in a third day of losses.

Representatives of Paytm and Ant Group didn’t respond to emails seeking comments.

The deal follows a surge of about 20% in Paytm’s shares this year. The rally received a boost after India earlier this month proposed easing rules on merchant fees for digital payments, while the company’s payments and financial services businesses have continued to perform better.

See also: China widens use of US$1.6 tril fund to spur spending on homes

Goldman Sachs Group Inc was the sole manager, the terms showed.

Later on Tuesday, exchange data showed domestic institutions, including SBI Mutual Fund, HDFC Mutual Fund were among buyers of Paytm shares while Integrated Core Strategies (Asia) Pte Ltd and MY Asian Opportunities Master Fund also acquired the firm’s shares via block trades.
